These ten hypotheses come from the 99 experiments, kept only where they also make architectural sense. The main pattern is that edits which create or protect a path from input to output help most when the parent lacks one. The evidence is weaker for hypotheses 8 to 10, mainly because few parents satisfy their conditions.

1. Setting edge 3 to skip_connect does better when edge 3 is currently none, because it adds a direct input-to-output path (parents 23, 26, 27).
2. Setting edge 3 to nor_conv_3x3 does better when edge 3 is currently none, for the same reason (parents 64, 67, 68, 69).
3. Setting edge 0 to none does worse when edge 3 is none, because edge 0 is then the main route to the output (parents 85, 88, 89).
4. Setting edge 5 to none does worse when edge 3 is none, since the output then depends on edges 4 and 5 (parents 95, 99).
5. Setting edge 2 to skip_connect does better when edge 1 is none, because it reconnects the 0 -> 2 -> 3 route (parents 73, 78).
6. Setting edge 2 to none does worse when edge 2 is currently nor_conv_3x3, because it removes a useful conv (parents 40, 46, 47, 48).
7. Setting edge 0 to none does worse when edge 2 is nor_conv_3x3, because a strong downstream conv loses its input (parents 80, 88, 89).
8. Setting edge 4 to nor_conv_3x3 does better when edge 4 is currently none, since it activates a dead edge (parents 53, 57, 58).
9. Setting edge 2 to skip_connect does better when edge 2 is currently none, since it adds a connection (parents 73, 78).
10. Setting edge 4 to nor_conv_3x3 does better when edge 1 is none, because edge 4 is then a key route to node 3 (parents 53, 57).
